Questions you can help answer.

We ranked twelve Millennium biology problems by public data, tractable computational progress, impact and a path to validation. Rubisco, cryopreservation and programmable proteases were selected for direct investigation.

These are research priorities, not probabilities of success. The work below was produced with Codex research agents and independently checked by other agents. It has not received external human expert review or experimental validation.

A concrete place to start

Our cryopreservation benchmark finds that changing the temperature interval used to judge warming rate reverses which heating schedule looks better. A constant schedule conditionally clears a thermal screen where the published ramp fails; the ramp is better over post-glass temperature windows.

This is a limited numerical result in a synthetic heart phantom. Its margin is small and depends on loading and boundary conditions. It does not demonstrate reduced ice, safe stress or organ recovery. Review rejected a separate inference about measured hearts; the corrected summary excludes it. General equal-iron spatial testing is prior art.

Ten more contributions, ready to review

Our next research batch contains five thermal comparisons, three Rubisco source and selection audits, and two protease analyses. Each has a defined question, code or source-linked evidence, results, limitations and a coordinator check. Positive findings and informative null results are both included.

All ten were produced by direct Codex CLI agents and checked again by the coordinating agent. None has received human acceptance or experimental validation. Two source audits require separately acquired third-party inputs for full re-extraction; their public checkers explain the narrower checks that can run from the repository alone.

Browse the ten result bundles ↗

Choose one claim, say exactly which version you checked, and share your evidence through a research-review issue. Your check, correction or replication keeps its own credit. The paper-card activity feed is separate from this GitHub research record.

Three useful contributions

  1. Reproduce the central comparison. Run the pinned model, state your environment and compare both schedules. An unsuccessful reproduction is useful if it includes the input version and failure.
  2. Test the boundary. Check whether the finding survives a documented alternative assumption. Keep model agreement separate from biological validation.
  3. Check priority or interpretation. Find earlier work with the same specific calculation, or identify an unsupported claim. Cite the exact source or code version.

Use your own GitHub account for authorship. Put code changes in a pull request and observations in an issue. Follow the review and credit process. No task is exclusively reserved; distinguish a fresh check from reusing someone else’s output.

Why these problems?

Scores use the median of three scouts’ judgments: 35% public data, 30% computational tractability, 20% impact and 15% validation path. Equal and validation-focused weights preserve the selected three. A stronger data weighting creates a third-place tie with regeneration.

The rest of the record matters too.

Rubisco work documents calibration and uncertainty provenance; it does not identify an improved enzyme. Reconstructing the authors’ corrected protease data weakened our initial raw-data error claim. A fixed time-course scoring hypothesis failed. Those corrections and negative results remain in the public research record.

Source links, original-code notices, reproduction instructions and model/refusal summaries are in the repository. Scientific claims should be cited to their original primary papers as well as the exact project version used.
